segments.voice: Yesterday: Kusha and Lava, named for a handful of grass, singing their father's story before him without knowing it. Today, the last time Sita stands before Rama.
screen: `TWO BOYS SING TO THEIR FATHER.`

segments.voice: Sita's name means furrow. Back in the first book, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual when the plow turned up a baby girl in the earth. He raised her as his daughter and named her for the furrow she was found in. Hold on to that, because the Ramayana remembers it. Today the girl from the furrow, now the mother of two grown boys, is brought before a great assembly and asked, one more time, to prove herself.
screen: `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `FOUND IN A PLOWED FIELD.` → `ASKED ONCE MORE TO PROVE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: When Rama learns the singing boys are his sons, he sends word to Valmiki: if Sita is pure, let her come and swear it here, before everyone, so the people can see. The next morning the assembly fills: sages, kings, ordinary people from every corner. Valmiki walks in first, and Sita follows, head bowed, hands folded. Valmiki speaks for her. These are your sons, he tells Rama, and Sita is blameless; he stakes on it all the merit of his long life of austerity. Rama answers that he believes it, and that he sent her away because of what people were saying. But the oath is still asked of her. Then Sita speaks. She makes three solemn declarations, each built the same way. If I have never thought of anyone but Rama, let the earth goddess open and give me a place. If I have honored him in mind, word and deed, let the earth receive me. As she finishes, the ground splits. A shining throne rises from below, held up by serpents, and the earth goddess herself takes Sita in her arms and seats her there. The throne sinks back down, and the earth closes. The assembly cries out. Rama is wild with grief, and angry at the earth itself. The girl found in a furrow has gone home to the ground she came from. And the poem doesn't say what to feel about it.

segments.voice: If you can, put your bare feet flat on the ground, or sit on the floor, and feel your weight handed down into the earth. You don't have to hold yourself up right now; the ground is doing it, and with each out-breath you can let a little more weight go down.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the girl from the furrow went home: Sita made her oath, and the earth opened and took her. Today, what the poets did next.
screen: `THE EARTH OPENS.`

segments.voice: A poet sits with a pen in the air. The poet loves this story, knows it by heart, and is retelling it for a new audience, in a new language, long after Valmiki. Now the ending has come: Sita's exile, and the earth opening. Tell it as it came down? Change it? Or quietly put the pen down before getting there? Real poets faced exactly this choice, and they didn't all choose the same way.
screen: `A POET, LONG AFTER VALMIKI.` → `YOU REACH THE ENDING.` → `TELL IT, CHANGE IT, OR STOP?`

segments.voice: Start with Bhavabhuti, a Sanskrit playwright. His play is called the Uttararamacharita, the later story of Rama. He follows the exile closely and lets Rama's grief run deep. But in the final act, Valmiki stages a play for Rama, a play about Sita, and when it ends, the earth goddess and the river Ganga bring Sita back, and husband and wife are reunited. Bhavabhuti changed the ending, inside the tradition, on purpose. Then there's Kamban, who sang the Ramayana in Tamil. His great poem closes with Rama's crowning; it doesn't go on into the later book. And Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a form of Hindi, and it's recited across North India today. His last section is also called the Uttar Kand, but it isn't a story of Sita's exile; it's mostly teaching and devotion, set in Rama's reign. So there are at least three moves inside the tradition itself: keep the hard ending and feel it fully, rewrite it toward reunion, or end the story at the crowning. None of these poets is outside the faith looking in. The tradition treasures them. That's why these days are called the tradition's own unresolved argument. It isn't critics against believers. It's the tradition arguing with itself, lovingly, and for a long time.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uttararamacharita, and the poets' three choices. Bhavabhuti rewrote the ending toward reunion, Kamban closed at the crowning, and Valmiki's text kept the earth opening. Today, the two sides of the argument itself.
screen: `TELL IT, CHANGE IT, OR STOP.`

segments.voice: A Ramayana play has ended, and a family is still at the dinner table. An uncle says Rama did the right thing: a king belongs to his people first. An aunt puts down her spoon and says Sita did nothing wrong, and she was sent away pregnant into a forest. A teenager asks why nobody asked Sita. Each of them is drawing on the tradition, and tables like that one are part of how the story lives. Today, the strongest form of each side, and Sita's own words from the text.
screen: `AFTER THE PLAY, AT THE TABLE.` → `HE WAS A KING FIRST.` → `SHE DID NOTHING WRONG.`

segments.voice: The first side rests on a Sanskrit idea: rajadharma, the duty of a king. In this reading, Rama's private life is not his own. A king who keeps what he loves while his people lose faith in him has failed the kingdom, so Rama gives up what is dearest to him, and suffers for it; the poem does show him suffering. Those who read it this way see the exile as a terrible sacrifice made by both of them, and honor it as such. The second side starts from Sita. She was already tested by fire, in the war book, and found pure. She is pregnant. She is sent away without a hearing, by a husband who knows she's innocent. Readers on this side, devotees of Rama among them, say this is a wound in the story, and they won't pretend it isn't. Some honor Sita as the true center of the poem. And then there are Sita's own words. When Lakshmana leaves her at the Ganga, Valmiki gives her a message to send back. She knows she is blameless, she says. She won't grieve for herself. She carries his child. And she asks Rama to care for the people of the city as he would his own brothers. There's no shouting in it, and a great deal of dignity. Women's songs in several Indian languages keep Sita's side alive, singing her grief in the forest. Both readings are inside the faith. Neither has won.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, rajadharma: the king's duty on one side, Sita's innocence on the other, and her own message sent back from the Ganga. Today, the last day of the Ramayana serial.
screen: `BOTH READINGS ARE INSIDE THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: One hundred eighty sessions ago, by a river, a hunter's arrow brought down a bird, and Valmiki's grief turned into the first verse. Since then: a bow broken at a wedding, a coronation canceled overnight, a forest, a golden deer, a leap across the sea, a war, a homecoming, and a later book that won't let the homecoming be the end. Today, the poem whole, and how the poem itself finally stops.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED EIGHTY SESSIONS.` → `FROM A BIRD'S CRY TO THE EARTH OPENING.` → `HOW DOES THE POEM STOP?`

segments.voice: Seven books. The Bala Kanda: childhood, the sage's errand, Sita's wedding. The Ayodhya Kanda: the throne promised and taken back, the exile, a father dying of grief, sandals on a throne. The Aranya Kanda: the forest, the golden deer, Sita carried off, Jatayu falling. The Kishkindha Kanda: Hanuman's first words, the alliance, the search. The Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, which many families recite on its own: the leap, the grove, Sita found. The Yuddha Kanda: the bridge, the war, the fire, the flight home. And the Uttara Kanda: the exile again, two sons, and the earth. After Sita is gone, Valmiki's poem goes on a little longer. Rama rules alone. Many years later, when his time on earth is complete, he walks into the river Sarayu, the people of Ayodhya follow him, and he returns to his divine form as Vishnu. That's the last image: a king walking into the water. And the tradition never stopped arguing about the chapter before it. Poets rewrote it. Reciters left it out. Devotees defended Rama, and devotees grieved for Sita, often the same devotees on different days. Calling the Uttara Kanda the tradition's own unresolved argument isn't a polite way of avoiding a verdict. It's a description. Many centuries of loving this story have not produced one answer, and the story is still sung.
screen: `SEVEN BOOKS, ONE POEM.` · `THE SUNDARA KANDA, RECITED ON ITS OWN.` · `RAMA WALKS INTO THE SARAYU.` · `THE ARGUMENT, STILL OPEN.` · then, large: `AND STILL THE STORY IS SUNG.`

670.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
670.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
670.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast through the day, sing devotional songs in the evening, and at midnight celebrate Krishna's birth with conch shells, bells and a decorated cradle, then break the fast.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarayu: the Ramayana serial ended with seven books, a king walking into the river, and a question still open. Today, a new block begins: the festival year.
screen: `SEVEN BOOKS. STILL SUNG.`

segments.voice: It's nearly midnight, and in temples across India, and in living rooms in Houston and Leicester and Singapore, people who have fasted all day are waiting. There's a small cradle decorated with flowers. Someone keeps checking the clock. At twelve, the conch shells blow, the bells ring, and somebody sets a tiny image of a baby into the cradle and starts rocking it. A birthday, kept at the exact hour. Why midnight? The answer starts in a prison cell.
screen: `A DAY OF FASTING.` → `AN EMPTY CRADLE.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: Janma means birth. Ashtami means the eighth: the eighth day of the waning moon. Janmashtami, the birthday on the eighth. The story is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana. In Mathura, the tyrant Kamsa is driving his cousin Devaki and her new husband Vasudeva in a chariot after their wedding, when a voice from the sky tells him: the eighth child of this woman will kill you. Kamsa locks them in prison. Child after child is born there, and Kamsa kills them; the seventh, the text says, is carried away to another womb. Then comes the eighth. He is born at midnight, in the dark half of the month, and the Bhagavata says the whole world grows calm and bright at that hour: rivers clear, fires burn steady, the sky full of stars. The baby first appears to his parents in a divine form, then becomes an ordinary newborn. Vasudeva's chains fall away. The guards sleep. The prison doors open by themselves. Vasudeva lifts the baby and walks out into a storm. The great serpent Shesha follows and spreads its hoods over them like an umbrella; in many tellings the baby rides in a basket on his head. At the Yamuna, swollen with rain, the river gives way to let him through. On the far bank is Gokul, where the cowherd Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth. Vasudeva leaves his son there and carries her baby back. By dawn, the prison doors are locked again, as if nothing happened. That's the night people stay up for: the good, arriving in the darkest hour, in the most locked-up place.

671.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
671.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
671.carry: welcome it, then let it go
671.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
671.howItsDone: Families bring a clay Ganesha home on Ganesh Chaturthi, install and worship it for one and a half to ten days with flowers, durva grass, modaks and aarti, then carry it in procession to water for immersion; many cities also hold large public pandals.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, a baby born at midnight in a prison and carried across a river in a storm. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Today, a guest arrives.
screen: `THE GOOD ARRIVES AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: In cities across Maharashtra, at the end of summer, you'll see something like a parade and a house move at once. A family walks down the street with drums and cymbals, and in the middle, carried on someone's head or in a car with the windows down, is a clay Ganesha, wrapped, garlanded, sometimes taller than the person carrying him. He's coming to stay: for a day and a half, or five days, or ten. And when he leaves, he won't go on a shelf. He'll be carried to the sea.
screen: `DRUMS IN THE STREET.` → `A CLAY GANESHA, CARRIED HOME.` → `AND THEN, TO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth: the fourth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, usually in August or September. It's kept as Ganesha's birthday; you met his birth story back in year one, the boy at the door. The festival has the shape of a guest's visit. First, the welcome. The clay image is set on a decorated altar at home, and in a rite called pranapratishtha, the giving of breath, the family invites the god to be present in it. From then on he's an honored guest. He's offered flowers, red hibiscus, durva grass, and modaks, the sweet dumplings he's said to love. People sing his aarti morning and evening; neighbors drop in to see him. Then, the farewell. On the last day, the family thanks him, and the image is carried in procession to a river, a lake or the sea, and immersed. That's called visarjan, letting go. The clay goes back to the water it came from. The public, street-sized version has a history too. In the 1890s, in Pune, the independence leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn a household festival into a public one, with shared pandals that brought whole neighborhoods together. Today some of those pandals draw crowds for days. And lately some families have chosen plain unbaked clay, so the image truly dissolves in the water.
screen: `CHATURTHI: THE FOURTH DAY.` · `THE WELCOME: BREATH GIVEN TO CLAY.` · `A GUEST, FED AND SUNG TO.` · `VISARJAN: GIVEN BACK TO THE WATER.` · then, large: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Hold something small you love in both hands, a mug, a photo, a stone, and look at it the way you'd look at a guest who's come a long way. Then set it down gently, and let your hands rest open in your lap.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day: a clay image welcomed home as a guest, honored, and given back to the water.
screen: `GANESH CHATURTHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Both halves are part of the honor. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 671 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NAVARATRI: NINE NIGHTS OF THE GODDESS.`

672.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
672.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
672.howItsDone: During autumn Navaratri, many Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, recitation of the Devi Mahatmya, garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, and golu doll displays in the South, ending with Vijayadashami on the tenth day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, a clay guest welcomed home and given back to the water. Your line was welcome it, then let it go. Today, a war the gods have already lost.
screen: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: The gods have lost. Not a skirmish: the whole war. A demon king named Mahisha, who can take the shape of a buffalo, has beaten them, thrown them out of heaven and taken their seats. They go, humiliated, to Vishnu and Shiva and tell them everything. And as they tell it, something happens that nobody plans. Their anger starts to glow. That's how the Devi Mahatmya, the great text of the Goddess, opens the battle it's known for.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE LOST.` → `MAHISHA TAKES HEAVEN.` → `THEIR ANGER STARTS TO GLOW.`

segments.voice: From the faces of Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma, and then from all the gods, a great light pours out, tejas, the text calls it, radiance, and it gathers into one blaze like a mountain on fire. The blaze takes the form of a woman: the Goddess. Every god gives her something: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, the mountain Himalaya a lion to ride. She laughs, and the sound shakes the worlds. Then she goes to war with Mahisha. He fights her as a buffalo, then a lion, then a man with a sword, then an elephant, then a buffalo again. She pins him under her foot, and as he tries to escape out of the buffalo's mouth in his true form, she ends him. In the Devi Mahatmya, that's one battle among several; she fights for the gods again and again. Navaratri means nine nights: nava, nine, ratri, night. For nine nights in autumn, in the month of Ashvin, many Hindus honor the Goddess, and how they do it changes as you cross India. In Gujarat, whole towns dance garba and dandiya in circles until late. In Bengal, it's Durga Puja, with huge clay images of Durga killing the buffalo demon. In much of the South, families set up golu, steps of dolls. On the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the day of victory, the good has won. And this week ends here: the earth opening, a poem argued over, a midnight birth, a clay guest, and now nine nights, and the dawn.
screen: `THE GODS' RADIANCE BECOMES ONE.` · `THE GODDESS, ARMED BY ALL.` · `MAHISHA CHANGES SHAPE; SHE WINS.` · `NAVA RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `ON THE TENTH DAY, VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing that keeps winning in you lately, a sharp word, scrolling past midnight, and name it silently, once. Then, as you breathe, say inwardly, not tonight, not as a battle but as a quiet decision, and let it rest in the body.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess in autumn, remembering how she defeated Mahisha, and ending on the tenth day, the day of victory.
screen: `NAVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. The tenth day belongs to victory. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 672 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DIWALI: THE ROW OF LAMPS.`
